stories.headline: SIR deletions raise questions as PAC chairpersons meet in Kerala
stories.summary: Two Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercises in Andhra Pradesh and Uttarakhand have come under scrutiny over process and transparency — journalists questioned the Andhra Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer's responses, while reporting from Uttarakhand said more than 2,700 names were deleted in the Gadarpur area on objections filed by poll officers after the prescribed deadline. In parallel, the Kerala Assembly is hosting a two-day conference of Public Accounts Committee chairpersons from 25 States, to be inaugurated by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, with around 300 MPs and MLAs expected to attend. The two developments together spotlight the twin axes of democratic accountability: due process in electoral roll revision by the Election Commission, and the strength of legislative financial oversight across the Union and the States.
stories.whyItMatters: It ties electoral-roll integrity and the ECI's Article 324 powers to parliamentary financial oversight — recurring GS-II themes on electoral governance, committee scrutiny and Union-State institutional dialogue.

perspectives.take: Frames the Andhra Pradesh SIR as a transparency deficit, arguing the CEO's statement failed to answer the specific questions raised by the outlet — a South Indian, accountability-focused lens.
Frames the Uttarakhand SIR as a due-process violation, highlighting deletions ordered on objections filed by poll officers after the deadline in Gadarpur.
Frames the Kerala PAC chairpersons' conference as an institutional-oversight and federal-cooperation story, foregrounding the scale of participation and the Speaker's role.

static.topic: Public Accounts Committee and Parliamentary Financial Oversight
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: The PAC is a parliamentary committee that examines the appropriation and finance accounts of the Union along with the audit reports of the CAG, verifying that money voted by Parliament was spent legally and effectively. It is a post-mortem, audit-based body and does not examine questions of policy.
static.background: Financial committees trace back to the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms, when the PAC was first constituted in India in 1921. It now has 22 members — 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha — elected by proportional representation by single transferable vote; by convention since 1967 the chairperson is drawn from the Opposition. Departmentally Related Standing Committees, set up in 1993, supplement this scrutiny of Bills and demands for grants.
static.whyInNews: The Kerala Assembly is hosting a two-day conference of PAC chairpersons from 25 States, to be inaugurated by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, with about 300 public representatives including MPs and MLAs expected to participate.
static.wayForward: Strengthen committee referral of Bills and audit follow-up, publish action-taken reports in the public domain, and institutionalise periodic Union–State committee exchanges so oversight keeps pace with the scale of public expenditure.
prelimsPointers: The PAC has 22 members — 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha — and by convention its chairperson has been from the Opposition since 1967.
The PAC examines CAG reports on appropriation and finance accounts but cannot question policy; it is distinct from the Estimates Committee and the Committee on Public Undertakings.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether parliamentary financial committees have kept pace with the scale and complexity of public expenditure, and suggest reforms for stronger audit follow-up.

static.topic: Electoral Roll Revision and Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Elections & Electoral Machinery
static.whatIsIt: The Election Commission of India, a constitutional body under Article 324, superintends the preparation and revision of electoral rolls. Besides the annual summary revision, it can undertake a more intensive, house-to-house Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in a State or district to remove dead, shifted, duplicate and otherwise ineligible entries.
static.background: Registration of electors is governed by the Representation of the People Act, 1950, with the Electoral Registration Officer as the statutory authority for additions and deletions; Article 326 provides for adult suffrage. Roll revision follows a prescribed cycle — draft roll publication, a claims-and-objections window, disposal by the ERO and final publication — with Form 6 (addition), Form 7 (objection) and Form 8 (correction) as the key forms.
static.socioEconomic: Deletions can affect welfare-linked documentation and political representation; procedural lapses risk disenfranchising genuine voters, making transparency and reasoned orders critical.
static.whyInNews: SIR exercises in Andhra Pradesh and Uttarakhand have drawn questions over the adequacy of official responses and over deletions ordered on objections filed after the deadline in Uttarakhand's Gadarpur area.
static.wayForward: Publish ward-wise deletion data with reasons, ensure objections are decided within the prescribed window through reasoned orders after hearing, and provide a robust appeal mechanism before final roll publication.
prelimsPointers: The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324; registration of voters is statutory under the RPA, 1950, while the conduct of elections is governed by the RPA, 1951.
Article 326 provides for elections on the basis of adult suffrage, and the ERO is the statutory authority to decide claims and objections to roll entries.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the balance between electoral roll purity and the right to franchise, and suggest procedural safeguards for intensive roll revision.

static.topic: Legislative Oversight and Cooperative Federalism
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India's quasi-federal arrangement divides powers through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule, with residuary powers vested in the Union under Article 248. Cooperative federalism is practised through institutions such as the Inter-State Council (Article 263), the GST Council, NITI Aayog and inter-legislative forums.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) examined the Centre–State balance, including the Governor's role under Articles 153, 200 and 201. Periodic friction over assent to State Bills and over fiscal devolution has kept the terms of cooperation under debate.
static.whyInNews: A conference of PAC chairpersons from 25 States hosted by the Kerala Assembly, with the Lok Sabha Speaker inaugurating it, is an instance of Union and State legislative institutions deliberating a shared oversight function.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise regular Union–State legislative and committee consultations, and route inter-governmental disputes through the Inter-State Council rather than ad hoc political negotiation.
prelimsPointers: On repugnancy in the Concurrent List, Union law prevails unless the State law has been reserved for and given the President's assent (Article 254).
The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory body for inter-State coordination and inquiry into disputes.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how inter-institutional dialogue among Union and State legislatures can strengthen cooperative federalism in India.

prelims: The Kerala Assembly is hosting a two-day conference of Public Accounts Committee chairpersons from 25 States; Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla is to inaugurate it, with about 300 MPs and MLAs expected.
In Uttarakhand's Gadarpur area, more than 2,700 names were deleted during the SIR on objections filed by poll officers after the deadline, according to Newslaundry.
The News Minute reported that the Andhra Pradesh CEO's statement did not answer its questions on the State's SIR.
Electoral roll revision is conducted by the ECI under Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
stories.mainsQuestion: The integrity of electoral rolls and the strength of legislative financial oversight are both tests of democratic accountability. In the light of recent Special Intensive Revision exercises and the conference of PAC chairpersons, examine the procedural safeguards needed to balance roll purity with the right to franchise. stories.headline: Scotch import probe clouds India-UK, India-EU trade momentum
stories.summary: India has opened a probe into imports of Scotch whisky from Britain, a move that has unsettled global liquor majors with large exposure to the Indian market and that lands in the middle of sensitive trade negotiations. Reuters frames the investigation as a commercial and diplomatic irritant, since whisky duties and market access are among the most contested chapters in India's talks with the UK. In parallel, the India-EU Free Trade Agreement negotiations — begun in 2007, repeatedly suspended, and concluded in New Delhi on 27 January 2026 according to a Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy analysis — have been billed by both sides as the largest trade deal either has signed. Legal-policy commentary suggests the enforcement of such deals is increasingly happening at the border through regulatory and customs action rather than through courts. Separately, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met India's Consul Generals in the United States, a consular-diplomacy engagement, while MobiKwik's record quarterly profit drove its shares up 10% — a markets story unconnected to the trade dispute.
stories.whyItMatters: Trade probes and non-tariff measures are now central to India's FTA bargaining, making regulatory decisions as consequential as tariff schedules for GS-II and GS-III answers on India's external economic policy.

perspectives.take: Frames the Scotch probe as an explainer-style commercial risk story: why an Indian investigation into British whisky imports is spooking global liquor companies and complicating trade diplomacy.

A legal-policy lens arguing that the India-EU FTA (talks from 2007, concluded 27 January 2026) shifts trade enforcement to the border rather than the courtroom — a domestic-institutions reading, not a market one.
Reports Jaishankar's meeting with India's Consul Generals in the US — a routine diplomatic-consular item, only tangentially linked to the trade story.
Market-focused and unrelated: MobiKwik shares jumping 10% on a record Rs 12 crore Q2 profit, illustrating business-press framing centred on earnings rather than policy.

static.topic: India–UK and India–EU Free Trade Agreements
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, Regional and Global Groupings and Agreements
static.whatIsIt: Comprehensive free trade agreements India is negotiating with the United Kingdom and the European Union, covering goods, services, investment, intellectual property and dispute settlement.
static.background: India–UK FTA negotiations were launched in January 2022. India–EU FTA talks originally began in 2007, were suspended for years, and were relaunched in 2022; per Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy, the negotiations concluded in New Delhi on 27 January 2026, with both sides calling it the largest trade agreement either has concluded.
static.socioEconomic: Alcohol beverages are among the most sensitive tariff lines for India because of large state excise revenues and a politically visible domestic liquor industry; UK and EU negotiators seek lower duties and stronger GI protection for Scotch and European spirits.
static.whyInNews: An Indian probe into Scotch whisky imports from Britain has rattled liquor majors and introduced friction into the trade negotiating track with the UK, even as the India–EU FTA has been brought to conclusion.
static.wayForward: Separate regulatory investigations from negotiating strategy, publish reasoned findings to preserve predictability for investors, and use GI and labelling standards transparently so that health or quality measures are not read as disguised protectionism.
prelimsPointers: India–UK FTA negotiations were launched in January 2022.
India–EU FTA talks began in 2007 and were relaunched in 2022 after a long suspension.
Scotch whisky is a UK geographical indication, protection for which is a standing demand in trade talks.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how regulatory and standards-based measures, rather than tariffs alone, determine outcomes in India's FTA negotiations with the UK and the EU.

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy and Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks, engaging simultaneously across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad (with the US, Japan and Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.socioEconomic: Economic diplomacy — trade agreements, investment treaties and market access — has become a core instrument of strategic autonomy, allowing India to deepen ties with Western partners without formal alliances.
static.whyInNews: The Scotch probe and the concluded India–EU FTA illustrate how commercial and regulatory decisions are now instruments of India's wider diplomatic balancing with the UK, the EU and the US.
static.wayForward: Keep trade and strategic tracks de-linked where possible, use economic agreements to lock in market access, and maintain consistency between domestic regulatory action and external commitments.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how economic diplomacy and trade agreements have become instruments of India's strategic autonomy in a multi-aligned world.

static.topic: Trade Remedies and Non-Tariff Barriers
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External Sector, Trade Policy
static.whatIsIt: Trade remedies are border measures — anti-dumping duties, countervailing duties, safeguards — plus standards, labelling and licensing rules that countries use to protect domestic industry within WTO rules.
static.background: India is among the most frequent users of anti-dumping measures at the WTO. Investigations are conducted by the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) under the commerce ministry, with findings notified by the finance ministry.
static.socioEconomic: Such measures protect domestic producers and revenue but raise consumer prices and can invite reciprocal action; they matter disproportionately for premium imported products such as Scotch whisky.
static.whyInNews: The reported Indian probe into Scotch imports is being read as a trade-remedy and standards action with direct consequences for foreign liquor companies and for ongoing FTA talks.
static.wayForward: Ensure investigations are time-bound, evidence-based and WTO-consistent, with reasoned public orders, so that legitimate domestic concerns do not translate into reputational costs in trade negotiations.
prelimsPointers: DGTR, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, conducts trade-remedy investigations in India.
Anti-dumping, countervailing and safeguard measures are the three principal WTO-permitted trade remedies.
static.mainsAngle: Are trade-remedy and standards-based measures becoming substitutes for tariffs in India's trade policy? Evaluate with reference to recent investigations and FTA negotiations.

prelims: India–UK FTA negotiations were launched in January 2022; India–EU FTA talks, begun in 2007, were relaunched in 2022 and concluded in New Delhi on 27 January 2026.
Scotch whisky is a UK geographical indication, and GI protection plus duty reduction are standing demands in India–UK and India–EU trade talks.
Trade-remedy investigations in India are conducted by the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) under the commerce ministry.
Alcoholic beverages are a high-revenue, heavily regulated sector in India, with states controlling excise and retail, making liquor a politically sensitive tariff line.
stories.mainsQuestion: Regulatory probes and standards, not tariffs alone, now decide the fate of trade negotiations. Examine this in the context of India's dealings with the UK and the EU, and suggest how India can balance domestic industry protection with credible trade commitments. (250 words)

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra coast; heavy rain alerts across five states
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu, a severe cyclonic storm over the Bay of Bengal, is forecast to make landfall near Ongole in Andhra Pradesh between midnight on Monday and Tuesday morning, triggering heavy-rain alerts across five states and the closure of schools in Chennai. The system arrives days after Cyclone Arnab left seven people dead, underlining how back-to-back cyclonic activity is stretching coastal preparedness this season. Coastal districts are braced for storm surge, wind damage and flooding, with state administrations issuing advisories and pre-positioning relief resources while central agencies coordinate warnings and response support. The event is a live test of India's multi-tier disaster architecture, running from IMD forecasts to state-level evacuation and specialised response force deployment.
stories.whyItMatters: Cyclone landfall sits at the intersection of GS-I physical geography (tropical cyclones, monsoon variability), GS-III disaster management and GS-II Centre–State coordination — all recurring UPSC themes.

perspectives.take: Frames it as a public-safety and logistics story — five-state rain alerts, Chennai school closures and precise landfall timing near Ongole; national-scope service journalism.
Places Murasu in a climate-vulnerability frame, linking it to Cyclone Arnab's seven deaths and questioning preparedness for successive extreme events on the Andhra coast.

static.topic: Tropical cyclones and the Indian monsoon system
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India (Monsoon, Tropical Cyclones)
static.whatIsIt: Tropical cyclones are warm-core low-pressure systems that form over warm ocean waters, drawing energy from latent heat released by condensation; in the North Indian Ocean they are called cyclones, and the Bay of Bengal is the more cyclone-prone of India's two adjoining seas.
static.background: The India Meteorological Department classifies North Indian Ocean systems by peak wind speed — cyclonic storm, severe cyclonic storm, very severe cyclonic storm, extremely severe cyclonic storm and super cyclone — and Bay of Bengal cyclones are named under a WMO/ESCAP panel of member countries. The monsoon itself is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the ITCZ shift and the Tibetan Plateau heat pump, delivering about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September; El Niño tends to weaken it, La Niña strengthens it, and the Indian Ocean Dipole modulates it.
static.geography: The Bay of Bengal's warm, relatively shallow waters and low-pressure troughs make it a cyclone nursery; the east coast — Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu — bears the brunt, while the Western Ghats and peninsular river systems shape inland flood behaviour.
static.socioEconomic: Cyclones cause loss of life, crop and aquaculture damage, power and transport disruption and displacement in densely populated coastal districts, straining state relief budgets and informal coastal livelihoods.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Murasu, a severe cyclonic storm, is forecast to make landfall near Ongole in Andhra Pradesh, with heavy rain alerts in five states and Chennai schools closed.
static.wayForward: Strengthen multi-hazard early warning and last-mile dissemination in local languages, build cyclone-resilient coastal infrastructure, and use ecosystem-based defences such as mangrove buffers.
prelimsPointers: IMD's 'severe cyclonic storm' category corresponds to wind speeds of roughly 89–117 kmph, between a cyclonic storm and a very severe cyclonic storm.
The Bay of Bengal accounts for the larger share of cyclones affecting India compared with the Arabian Sea.
Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed) while peninsular rivers are largely rain-fed and seasonal.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how cyclone frequency and intensity in the North Indian Ocean interact with monsoon variability and climate change, and assess India's coastal disaster preparedness.

static.topic: Centre–State coordination in disaster response
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: Disaster management is not a separately enumerated subject in the Seventh Schedule; the Disaster Management Act, 2005 supplies the statutory framework, with states handling relief and rehabilitation within their territory while the Union supports through funds, advisories and specialised central forces.
static.background: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Art. 248). The Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined the Centre–State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201).
static.socioEconomic: Disaster relief is fiscally heavy for coastal states; central assistance routed through the National Disaster Response Fund and State Disaster Response Funds largely determines how quickly relief reaches affected households.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Murasu's landfall warning near Ongole involves coordinated advisories, evacuation and resource deployment across five states and the Union government.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise pre-monsoon inter-agency drills, clarify funding timelines, and strengthen State and District Disaster Management Authorities for faster last-mile action.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless the state law is reserved for the President's assent (Art. 254).
The Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Recent spats over Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess cooperative federalism in practice, including in disaster response.

static.topic: India's disaster management architecture
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — Institutional Framework
static.whatIsIt: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 created the National Disaster Management Authority (chaired by the Prime Minister), State Disaster Management Authorities (chaired by Chief Ministers) and District Disaster Management Authorities, with the National Disaster Response Force as the specialised response force.
static.background: The Act followed the 1999 Odisha super cyclone and the 2001 Bhuj earthquake, shifting policy emphasis from relief-centric response towards prevention, mitigation and preparedness. India is a signatory to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030).
static.socioEconomic: Cyclone response involves evacuation of coastal populations, shelter management and compensation, financed through the National Disaster Response Fund and State Disaster Response Funds.
static.whyInNews: Pre-landfall mobilisation for Cyclone Murasu — warnings, school closures and evacuation advisories — is a live test of this framework.
static.wayForward: Move from response to risk-informed planning: cyclone shelters, mangrove buffers, enforcement of building codes and community-based early warning.
prelimsPointers: NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister; the SDMA is chaired by the Chief Minister.
The NDRF is the specialised response force constituted under the disaster management framework.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's disaster management framework has shifted adequately from relief-centric response to risk reduction.

Heavy rain alerts were issued across five states, and schools were closed in Chennai.
The storm follows Cyclone Arnab, which left seven people dead.
IMD's 'severe cyclonic storm' category corresponds to wind speeds of about 89–117 kmph.
stories.mainsQuestion: Cyclones in the Bay of Bengal are recurring, high-impact hazards. Discuss how India's disaster management framework and Centre–State coordination shape the effectiveness of pre-landfall preparedness, using recent cyclonic events as illustrations.

stories.headline: Sensex rallies on Reliance as Q2 earnings and AI sell-off dominate
stories.summary: Indian equities extended gains on Monday, with the Sensex and Nifty holding firmly higher on the back of Reliance Industries and energy stocks, even as IT and pharma counters weakened. The session ran alongside a heavy Q2 FY27 earnings day: Escorts Kubota reported a 20% year-on-year fall in profit after tax, MobiKwik turned profitable and Devyani International's loss narrowed, while ITC, Marico, UPL, Petronet LNG, NLC, DOMS, NALCO, Wockhardt and Granules were among those due to report. Separately, SK Finance reported H1 FY27 PAT up 25% to ₹225 crore, and Japan's Sumitomo lifted its FY26 profit and dividend forecasts on strong energy and metals performance. Globally, attention turned to whether the AI investment boom is losing steam, with Business Standard examining the drivers of the ongoing sell-off in AI-linked shares. The RBI's daily money market operations release for November 1, 2026 recorded nil volumes in the overnight segment.
stories.whyItMatters: Earnings season, index-level sector rotation and global AI-linked volatility are recurring themes for GS-III economy questions on capital markets, corporate performance and external shocks. static.topic: Indian Capital Markets and SEBI Regulation
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Capital Markets and Financial Sector Regulation
static.whatIsIt: India's securities market has a primary segment (IPOs, bonds) and a secondary segment (exchange trading), regulated by SEBI. The BSE (1875) and NSE (1992) are the principal exchanges; the Sensex (30 stocks, launched 1986) and Nifty 50 (launched 1996) are the benchmark indices.
static.background: SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory powers by the SEBI Act, 1992, in the aftermath of the Harshad Mehta securities scam. Dematerialisation through NSDL (1996) and CDSL (1999), the introduction of equity derivatives (2000), rolling settlement and the shift to T+1 settlement (2023) progressively modernised market infrastructure. Foreign portfolio investment and domestic institutional flows, including SIP-driven mutual fund inflows, now materially influence index movement.
static.socioEconomic: Retail participation expanded sharply after 2020 through demat accounts and systematic investment plans, tying household savings more closely to market volatility and to insurance and pension portfolios.
static.whyInNews: The Sensex and Nifty extended gains led by Reliance Industries and energy stocks, while IT and pharma shares weakened — an illustration of sector rotation within the index.
static.wayForward: Deepen the corporate bond market, strengthen disclosure and investor-protection norms, and expand financial literacy so that rising retail participation does not translate into concentrated risk-taking.
prelimsPointers: Sensex is the 30-stock benchmark index of the BSE; Nifty 50 is the benchmark index of the NSE.
SEBI, created in 1988, became a statutory body under the SEBI Act, 1992.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate SEBI's dual mandate of market development and investor protection in the context of rising retail participation and global volatility spillovers.

static.topic: Quarterly Earnings and Corporate Disclosure Norms
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Corporate Sector, Financial Reporting and Transparency
static.whatIsIt: Listed companies must disclose unaudited quarterly financial results under the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. Profit after tax (PAT) is the headline profitability metric, and year-on-year comparison is the standard performance yardstick.
static.background: Quarterly reporting was earlier governed by Clause 41 of the listing agreement; the LODR Regulations, 2015 consolidated and tightened these obligations. Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), converged with IFRS, became applicable to major listed companies from FY2016-17. The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) was later mandated for the top listed companies by market capitalisation.
static.socioEconomic: Earnings outcomes influence index levels, corporate tax collections, capex and hiring decisions, and the savings of retail investors holding equity directly or through mutual funds.
static.whyInNews: A dense Q2 FY27 results day: Escorts Kubota's PAT fell 20% year-on-year, MobiKwik posted a profit, Devyani International's loss narrowed, and ITC, Marico, UPL, Petronet LNG, NLC, DOMS, NALCO, Wockhardt and Granules were scheduled to announce results.
static.wayForward: Improve the quality and comparability of disclosures, strengthen assurance over non-financial reporting, and reduce information asymmetry for retail investors.
prelimsPointers: Under SEBI LODR Regulations, listed entities file quarterly results within 45 days of the end of the quarter.
BRSR disclosure is mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation.
static.mainsAngle: How do corporate earnings cycles and disclosure standards shape capital formation and investor confidence in the Indian economy?

static.topic: The Global AI Investment Boom and Market Correction
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Global Markets, Technology and Industrial Policy
static.whatIsIt: The AI investment cycle refers to large-scale capital expenditure by technology hyperscalers and their suppliers on data centres, advanced semiconductors (GPUs) and power infrastructure, which has driven global equity valuations in AI-linked companies.
static.background: Since the rapid diffusion of large language models from 2022-23, AI-linked equities led global indices, creating valuation concentration in a few mega-cap firms. Periodic corrections have followed questions over the returns on this capex and over monetisation timelines. The semiconductor supply chain — concentrated in Taiwan, South Korea and the Netherlands — is central to the cycle.
static.geography: Semiconductor fabrication and advanced packaging capacity is concentrated in East Asia, with critical lithography equipment supplied from Europe, making the AI supply chain geographically concentrated and geopolitically exposed.
static.socioEconomic: AI-linked valuation swings affect global capital flows into emerging markets such as India, currency movements, and demand for Indian IT services exports.
static.whyInNews: Business Standard examined whether the AI investment boom is losing steam and what is driving the sell-off, a theme that coincided with weakness in Indian IT and pharma shares.
static.wayForward: Diversify export baskets, build domestic semiconductor and AI capability through the India Semiconductor Mission and the IndiaAI Mission, and monitor capital-flow volatility arising from global technology cycles.
prelimsPointers: The India Semiconductor Mission was launched in 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore.
The IndiaAI Mission was approved in 2024 with an outlay of about ₹10,372 crore.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the global AI investment cycle and its periodic corrections affect India's technology exports, capital flows and industrial policy priorities.

stories.mainsQuestion: Corporate earnings cycles and global technology-driven valuation swings increasingly shape Indian equity markets. Examine how such developments influence capital formation, retail investor behaviour and India's broader macroeconomic stability, and suggest safeguards.

stories.headline: Delhi's air quality worsens as GRAP anti-pollution curbs come into force
stories.summary: New Delhi's air quality deteriorated as emergency anti-pollution measures under the Graded Response Action Plan began operating in the capital, according to Reuters. The report frames the decline as the onset of the annual winter pollution episode, when meteorological conditions trap emissions close to the ground. Curbs on construction, vehicular movement and other dust- and emission-generating activities are the standard first-line response in the Delhi-NCR region. The episode again highlights the gap between episodic, AQI-triggered action and the year-round, source-level control that the region's airshed requires.
stories.whyItMatters: Winter air pollution in Delhi-NCR is a recurring UPSC theme linking environmental governance, inter-state coordination, judicial intervention and public health. It tests understanding of GRAP, CAQM, NCAP and the Air Act framework, plus the geography of the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

perspectives.take: Frames the story as a seasonal public-health and governance event — deteriorating air quality despite the activation of official anti-pollution measures; a global wire-service lens emphasising official response and health impact rather than domestic political blame.

static.topic: Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)
static.syllabusNode: Environment — pollution control institutions and air quality governance
static.whatIsIt: GRAP is an emergency, graded set of anti-pollution measures for Delhi-NCR that is triggered automatically as air quality crosses defined AQI thresholds, escalating from the lower stages up to the 'Severe+' category. It is implemented and monitored by the CAQM, which also issues directions to state agencies.
static.background: GRAP was first notified in 2017 by the CPCB on the directions of the Supreme Court in the M.C. Mehta v. Union of India line of cases, and was initially overseen by the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA). EPCA was replaced by the CAQM, created first through an ordinance in 2020 and then given statutory backing by the CAQM Act, 2021, whose jurisdiction covers Delhi and specified NCR districts of Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.
static.geography: Delhi sits in the landlocked Indo-Gangetic Plain. In winter, low surface temperatures, a shallow mixing height, calm winds and temperature inversion trap pollutants near the ground, while the Himalayas to the north restrict dispersal — so local and regional emissions accumulate over the same airshed.
static.socioEconomic: Severe episodes impose a respiratory and cardiovascular health burden, especially on children, the elderly and outdoor workers; construction bans and transport restrictions disrupt livelihoods, real-estate activity and informal employment, creating a recurring tension between emergency health protection and economic activity.
static.whyInNews: Air quality in New Delhi deteriorated as the anti-pollution measures under the graded framework took effect, marking the start of the winter pollution season.
static.wayForward: Shift from episodic, AQI-triggered curbs to year-round, source-apportioned action across the whole NCR airshed; strengthen regional coordination, public transport, mechanised road sweeping, waste management and crop-residue alternatives; improve real-time monitoring and enforcement capacity.
prelimsPointers: GRAP measures escalate in stages as AQI worsens, with the strictest stage applied at 'Severe+' levels.
CAQM is a statutory body under the CAQM Act, 2021, covering Delhi and NCR districts of Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.
GRAP was originally notified in 2017 on Supreme Court directions and was earlier administered by the EPCA.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether emergency, threshold-based action plans can deliver durable air quality improvement, or whether they must be complemented by structural, airshed-level reforms.

static.topic: National Clean Air Programme (NCAP)
static.syllabusNode: Environment — air pollution policy and urban environmental management
static.whatIsIt: NCAP is the Centre's long-term framework for reducing ambient particulate pollution in identified non-attainment cities, using city-specific action plans, monitoring networks and performance-linked funding.
static.background: Launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in 2019, NCAP initially targeted a 20–30% reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations by 2024 over a 2017 base year across 131 non-attainment cities. The target was subsequently revised upward to a 40% reduction in particulate concentrations by 2025-26. The Fifteenth Finance Commission also tied air quality grants to cities meeting pollution-reduction milestones.
static.geography: Non-attainment cities are spread across the Indo-Gangetic Plain and peninsular India, with the worst concentrations typically in northern inland cities where winter meteorology limits dispersion.
static.socioEconomic: Air pollution imposes productivity losses, higher healthcare expenditure and reduced life expectancy; NCAP funding is intended to build institutional capacity in municipal bodies that often lack technical staff.
static.whyInNews: The winter deterioration in Delhi-NCR renews scrutiny of whether NCAP's medium-term targets are translating into measurable on-ground improvement.
static.wayForward: Link disbursal of funds more tightly to verified emission reductions, expand monitoring to smaller towns, and integrate NCAP city plans with regional airshed plans.
keyTerms: Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations
prelimsPointers: NCAP was launched in 2019 and originally covered 131 non-attainment cities.
The particulate reduction target was revised to 40% by 2025-26 over the 2017 base year.
The Fifteenth Finance Commission provided air quality grants to million-plus cities tied to performance.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the institutional and financial constraints that limit the effectiveness of the National Clean Air Programme in non-attainment cities.

static.topic: Crop residue (stubble) burning and its regulation
static.syllabusNode: Environment — agricultural pollution and regional air quality
static.whatIsIt: Post-harvest burning of paddy residue, mainly in Punjab and Haryana, releases particulate matter and gases that contribute to winter pollution in the Delhi-NCR airshed.
static.background: The practice intensified after the mid-2000s with the shift to short-duration paddy varieties and delayed sowing cycles that leave a narrow window between paddy harvest and wheat sowing. Responses have included the CAQM's directions, the Crop Residue Management scheme for machinery such as happy seeders and super straw management systems, the Pusa bio-decomposer, and Supreme Court monitoring.
static.geography: Punjab and Haryana lie upwind of Delhi during the post-monsoon north-westerly wind regime, so emissions from the two states are transported into the NCR.
static.socioEconomic: Farmers face high costs of residue removal and machinery rental against a short sowing window; alternatives must be economically viable, not merely technically available.
static.whyInNews: Stubble burning is a recurring contributor to the winter spike in Delhi-NCR pollution that triggers GRAP measures.
static.wayForward: Diversify cropping patterns, strengthen residue-to-energy and residue-to-fodder value chains, ensure timely and adequate compensation for machinery, and coordinate across state boundaries.
prelimsPointers: Paddy residue burning peaks in the post-monsoon period in Punjab and Haryana.
The Crop Residue Management scheme subsidises machinery for in-situ and ex-situ residue management.
The Pusa bio-decomposer is a microbial solution developed by ICAR-IARI for in-situ straw decomposition.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why crop residue burning persists despite regulatory and technological interventions, and suggest economically viable alternatives.

prelims: GRAP is an emergency, AQI-threshold-based action plan for Delhi-NCR, implemented by the CAQM.
CAQM is a statutory body under the CAQM Act, 2021, with jurisdiction over Delhi and NCR districts of Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.
Winter pollution in Delhi is aggravated by temperature inversion, low mixing height and calm winds over the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
NCAP, launched in 2019, targets a 40% reduction in particulate concentrations by 2025-26 over the 2017 base year.
stories.mainsQuestion: Emergency measures under the Graded Response Action Plan are activated every winter, yet Delhi-NCR's air quality continues to deteriorate. Critically examine the reasons for this gap and suggest institutional and structural reforms for airshed-level air quality management.

stories.headline: BJP, Congress clash over Ramlila Maidan rally, AI photo and festive trade losses
stories.summary: The INDIA bloc held a rally at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi on 1 November against the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and alleged 'vote chori', triggering a sharp political exchange with the BJP. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi alleged that Connaught Place shops were forcibly shut during the rally, while his party contended that traders gained from the mobilisation; the traders' body CTI claimed losses of ₹10,000–11,000 crore across Delhi markets. BJP leaders countered that the opposition had ignored traders' pleas, and the two sides also sparred over an AI-generated photograph linked to the rally. Separately, Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi met RJD chief Lalu Prasad Yadav in New Delhi, with the two recalling the UPA era and laws such as MGNREGA, RTE and RTI — read as a signal of continuing opposition outreach.
stories.whyItMatters: Ties together electoral-roll revision and election-integrity debates, protest politics in the capital, the commercial cost of mass mobilisation, and opposition alliance-building — all recurring GS-II (elections, Parliament, welfare legislation) themes.

perspectives.take: Frames the episode as a two-way political slanging match over the rally, an AI-generated photograph and festive business losses — a national-desk horse-race read.
Hindi, ground-reporting framing: asks whether 'vote chori'/SIR was the only issue on people's minds, sceptical of single-issue protest narratives.
Business-desk emphasis on the commercial fallout, centring the ₹10,000–11,000 crore loss claim by CTI and the blame game over Connaught Place closures.
Carries the PTI report on Sonia Gandhi meeting Lalu Prasad, framing it as opposition consolidation and UPA-legacy nostalgia rather than the Delhi rally row.

static.topic: UPA-era rights-based laws and their welfare legacy (MGNREGA, RTE, RTI)
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare Schemes and Rights-based Legislation
static.whatIsIt: India's rights-based welfare framework: MGNREGA (2005) guaranteeing 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household a year, the RTE Act (2009) making elementary education a fundamental right under Article 21A, and the RTI Act (2005) providing access to public records. Delivery is increasingly routed through DBT on the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone.
static.background: Recalled in the Sonia Gandhi–Lalu Prasad meeting, which invoked the UPA era during which these laws were enacted. The rights-based shift followed the 2004 mandate and the National Common Minimum Programme; the architecture later expanded to the NFSA 2013, Ayushman Bharat (2018, with its PM-JAY insurance arm and Health and Wellness Centres), POSHAN Abhiyaan, and four labour codes consolidating 29 labour laws.
static.socioEconomic: Rights-based entitlements raised rural wage floors and school enrolment, but current debates focus on exclusion errors, urban poverty and a shift from entitlement to capability.
static.whyInNews: ThePrint reported that Sonia Gandhi and RJD chief Lalu Prasad Yadav met at MP Misa Bharti's residence in New Delhi and reminisced about the UPA era and the implementation of laws like MGNREGA, RTE and RTI.
static.wayForward: Strengthen last-mile delivery and grievance redress to cut exclusion errors, index benefits to inflation, and widen social-security coverage for urban informal workers.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 existing labour laws.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how rights-based welfare legislation has changed the character of Indian social policy, and identify the institutional gaps in its implementation.

static.topic: Electoral roll revision and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Elections, Election Commission and Electoral Reforms
static.whatIsIt: Electoral rolls are prepared and revised by the Election Commission under Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act, 1950. A Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is a more intensive, house-to-house verification of existing roll entries, distinct from routine annual or quarterly revision, with Form 6 for new voters and deletion of ineligible, duplicate or deceased entries after notice and hearing.
static.background: The Election Commission has conducted intensive roll-verification exercises in phases, including in Bihar in 2025, using door-to-door enumeration and qualifying-date revisions. Roll-revision disputes have repeatedly gone to court, with deletion protocols and notice requirements being the main contested points.
static.geography: Ramlila Maidan and Connaught Place in central Delhi — venues of the INDIA bloc rally and of traders' claims of losses during it.
static.socioEconomic: Balancing roll purity against the risk of disenfranchisement; large mobilisations in central Delhi also impose measurable commercial costs on nearby markets.
static.whyInNews: The INDIA bloc rally at Ramlila Maidan was held against the SIR/roll-revision exercise and alleged 'vote chori', sparking charges and counter-charges between the BJP and Congress.
static.wayForward: Publish transparent, auditable SIR protocols with clear deletion criteria, time-bound appeals and error-correction, so that roll accuracy is achieved without large-scale disenfranchisement.
prelimsPointers: The Election Commission is a constitutional body under Article 324; electoral rolls are prepared under the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
Form 6 is used for new voter registration; deletions from rolls must follow notice and an opportunity of hearing.
static.mainsAngle: Electoral roll revision is central to electoral credibility yet frequently becomes a political flashpoint. Examine the institutional safeguards available to ensure a transparent, error-free revision.

static.topic: Opposition politics, parliamentary accountability and legislating social rights
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament and the Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Parliament (Article 79) consists of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha; a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha, and ordinances (Article 123) may be promulgated when Parliament is not in session, requiring approval within six weeks of reassembly.
static.background: The laws invoked in the Sonia Gandhi–Lalu Prasad meeting were products of the UPA-era legislative pipeline. Scrutiny today largely flows through Departmentally Related Standing Committees, and instruments such as the guillotine, Zero Hour and no-confidence motions shape parliamentary accountability.
static.whyInNews: ThePrint's report on the Sonia Gandhi–Lalu Prasad meeting, recalling UPA-era legislation, places the opposition's legislative record and alliance-building at the centre of current political commentary.
static.wayForward: Restore committee referral rates and floor debate time so that major social legislation is scrutinised rather than guillotined.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how declining committee referrals and shrinking sitting days affect the quality of legislation on social rights.

prelims: The INDIA bloc rally was held at Ramlila Maidan, Delhi, on 1 November against the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and alleged 'vote chori'.
The traders' body CTI claimed losses of ₹10,000–11,000 crore across Delhi markets during the rally period, while Rahul Gandhi alleged Connaught Place shops were forcibly shut.
The Election Commission is a constitutional body under Article 324; electoral rolls are prepared and revised under the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year — one of the UPA-era laws recalled in the Sonia Gandhi–Lalu Prasad meeting.
stories.mainsQuestion: Electoral roll revision is essential to electoral credibility but repeatedly becomes a flashpoint between ruling and opposition parties. Examine the institutional safeguards under Article 324 and the Representation of the People Acts that can make such revisions transparent, error-free and non-disenfranchising.

stories.headline: Supreme Court seeks stronger teeth for curbs on courtroom clips
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has signalled that it wants its restrictions on the circulation of clips drawn from live-streamed court proceedings to carry real enforcement force, rather than remain advisory. The push follows concern that edited or commercialised excerpts of hearings can distort judicial proceedings even as live-streaming itself is defended as a step toward open justice. In a reflective companion account, the Supreme Court Observer revisits the working of the collegium, the body of judges that appoints judges, throwing light on how appointment deliberations are conducted behind closed doors. Separately, in a decision reported by Bar & Bench, the Supreme Court set aside the Rajasthan State Election Commission's refusal to permit a civil society group to run awareness campaigns, reaffirming that civic speech around elections enjoys constitutional protection and that refusals must be reasoned and proportionate. Read together, the two strands show the apex court tightening control over its own broadcast footprint while expanding the space for civic expression.
stories.whyItMatters: The story tests two core UPSC themes at once: the contours of open justice and court regulation of its own proceedings, and the constitutional limits on restricting speech, including during elections. It also offers current material on the collegium, judicial transparency and the Election Commission's regulatory reach.

perspectives.take: Frames the issue as the Court wanting enforcement 'teeth' in its guidelines on clips of live-streamed hearings, treating misuse and distortion, rather than live-streaming itself, as the problem to be fixed.

The collegium piece is an insider, process-oriented account of judicial appointments, read as a candid institutional memoir rather than advocacy; useful as context on the opacity debate surrounding judicial selection.

Court-reporting lens on a free-speech remedy: the Supreme Court quashing the Rajasthan State Election Commission's refusal to allow a civil society group's awareness campaigns, stressing reasoned decision-making by electoral authorities.

static.topic: Live-streaming of court proceedings and regulation of courtroom clips
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: transparency, open justice and court regulation of proceedings
static.whatIsIt: Live-streaming is the real-time broadcast of hearings, chiefly of the Supreme Court and several High Courts. The Court's current concern is not the streaming itself but the downstream use of short clips cut from those streams, which the Court wishes to bring under enforceable restrictions.
static.background: The Supreme Court allowed live-streaming of its proceedings in Swapnil Tripathi v. Union of India (2018), reasoning that access to justice and judicial transparency are served by opening hearings to a wider audience. The Court subsequently notified dedicated live-streaming rules (2021) covering Constitutional Bench and other specified matters, and several High Courts began streaming through the eCourts and court-website/YouTube arrangements. Practice since then has raised questions of misleading edits, unauthorised commercial exploitation and prejudicial use of clips during pending matters.
static.geography: Operates India-wide; applies directly to Supreme Court proceedings and influences the live-streaming experiments of High Courts and tribunals.
static.socioEconomic: Digital access to hearings widens public understanding of the judiciary and legal literacy, but the benefits depend on connectivity, language access and responsible reuse of broadcast material.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court indicated it wants stronger, enforceable curbs on clips drawn from its live streams, prompting debate on how far regulation of broadcast excerpts can go without diluting the transparency that justified streaming in the first place.
static.wayForward: Codified clip-use norms with clear attribution requirements; prescribed formats for certified excerpts and transcripts; graded consequences for distorting edits; a distinction between journalistic, educational and commercial use; and periodic review of the live-streaming rules in consultation with press and bar bodies.
keyTerms: Right to know vs. fair trial
prelimsPointers: Live-streaming of Supreme Court proceedings was authorised by the Court in Swapnil Tripathi v. Union of India (2018).
Article 129 makes the Supreme Court a court of record with the power to punish for contempt, which underpins its authority to regulate misuse of its proceedings' broadcast material.
Broadcast and expression of court proceedings sit against Article 19(1)(a), subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether live-streaming and clip circulation advance open justice or create new risks to fair trial and judicial dignity, and suggest a balanced regulatory framework.

static.topic: Collegium system and appointment of judges
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: appointment and independence of judges
static.whatIsIt: The collegium is the body of senior Supreme Court judges that recommends appointments and transfers of judges to the Supreme Court and High Courts. For Supreme Court appointments it is the Chief Justice of India with the four senior-most puisne judges; for High Court appointments, the CJI with two senior-most judges, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court and the Governor.
static.background: The collegium system is a judicial creation, not a constitutional text: it evolved through the Three Judges Cases — S.P. Gupta (1981), the Second Judges Case (1993) and the Third Judges Case (1998 advisory opinion under Article 143). The 99th Constitutional Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 were struck down in 2015 for violating the basic structure. A Memorandum of Procedure to streamline appointments has long been under discussion.
static.socioEconomic: Debate centres on judicial independence versus accountability, transparency of selection criteria and representativeness of the bench, including social diversity.
static.whyInNews: A reflective account of collegium deliberations has renewed public discussion on how judicial appointments are actually decided and why the process remains largely confidential.
static.wayForward: Finalising the Memorandum of Procedure, publishing reasoned appointment criteria, fixed timelines for recommendations and executive action, and structured disclosure without compromising confidentiality of deliberations.
prelimsPointers: The NJAC was created by the 99th Constitutional Amendment and the NJAC Act, 2014, both struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.
The collegium's composition was clarified in the Third Judges Case (1998), an advisory opinion under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Critically assess the collegium system: has it secured judicial independence at the cost of transparency and accountability? Suggest reforms consistent with the basic structure.

static.topic: Freedom of speech in electoral awareness campaigns
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights (Article 19) and Elections (Article 324)
static.whatIsIt: The case concerns a State Election Commission's refusal to permit a civil society group to conduct voter or civic awareness campaigns, and the Supreme Court's setting aside of that refusal.
static.background: Speech and expression are protected under Article 19(1)(a), with reasonable restrictions permitted under Article 19(2). Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission, and the Model Code of Conduct — a non-statutory, consensus instrument — governs campaign conduct. The Election Commission's own Systematic Voters' Education and Electoral Participation (SVEEP) programme is the institutional channel for voter awareness.
static.geography: Rajasthan-specific dispute with All-India significance for how State Election Commissions treat civil society campaigns.
static.socioEconomic: Civil society awareness drives influence turnout and voter information, particularly among first-time, rural and marginalised voters; restrictions on them bear directly on democratic participation.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court set aside the Rajasthan State Election Commission's refusal to allow a civil society group's awareness campaigns, in Bar & Bench's report of the decision.
static.wayForward: Reasoned, speaking orders for any refusal; proportionate and content-neutral restrictions rather than blanket bans; transparent criteria for permitting civil society campaigns; and clear coordination between the Election Commission and such groups.
prelimsPointers: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India.
The Model Code of Conduct is not a statutory enactment but operates by consensus among political parties.
SVEEP is the Election Commission's flagship voter education and awareness programme.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the constitutional limits on electoral authorities' power to restrict civic awareness campaigns, and the standards of reasoned and proportionate decision-making such refusals must satisfy.

prelims: Live-streaming of Supreme Court proceedings was authorised in Swapnil Tripathi v. Union of India (2018); the Court later notified dedicated live-streaming rules covering Constitutional Bench and other specified matters.
The Supreme Court is a court of record under Article 129 and holds contempt power, which is relevant to regulating misuse of clips of its proceedings.
In a separate ruling, the Supreme Court set aside the Rajasthan State Election Commission's refusal to allow a civil society group to conduct awareness campaigns.
The collegium system rests on the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); the NJAC, created by the 99th Amendment, was struck down in 2015.
stories.mainsQuestion: Live-streaming of judicial proceedings is defended as an instrument of open justice, yet unregulated circulation of courtroom clips can distort hearings and prejudice pending matters. Examine the balance between judicial transparency and the administration of justice, and suggest safeguards for responsible reuse of court broadcast material.

stories.headline: Sal borer outbreak, insect stress and hidden coastal risks spotlight ecological vulnerabilities
stories.summary: A renewed sal borer infestation in Madhya Pradesh’s Dindori forests has led to the felling of more than 45,000 trees, with officials ordering a fresh survey as the outbreak appears worse than last year. A separate report says lowland insects are under stress, pointing to wider pressures on invertebrate biodiversity. Scroll.in has launched a public-interest investigation into coastal construction risks that builders may be concealing from apartment buyers. Taken together, the developments highlight forest health, insect decline and coastal hazard transparency as linked environmental governance concerns.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, these issues connect to biodiversity conservation, forest pest management, climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction and regulatory transparency in coastal zones.

perspectives.take: Frames the sal borer outbreak as a worsening forest emergency in Madhya Pradesh and separately flags lowland insects as under stress, emphasising ecological damage and biodiversity loss.

static.topic: Biodiversity, Wetlands & Conservation

static.whatIsIt: India is one of 17 megadiverse countries. Key instruments include the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Biological Diversity Act 2002, Forest Conservation Act 1980, and the CBD (1992) with its Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022).
static.background: Ramsar Convention (1971) protects wetlands; India has 80+ Ramsar sites. Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) anchor species conservation. The 30x30 target aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
static.geography: India's biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland/Nicobar.
static.socioEconomic: Ecosystem services support livelihoods, but conservation often competes with development and community rights.
static.whyInNews: The sal borer outbreak and reported stress on lowland insects highlight pressures on forest health and invertebrate biodiversity.

static.topic: Forest Pest Outbreaks and Forest Health
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Forests & Biodiversity
static.whatIsIt: Forest pest outbreaks, such as sal borer in sal forests, can cause large-scale tree mortality and trigger sanitation felling.
static.background: Indian forest governance operates under the Indian Forest Act 1927, Forest Conservation Act 1980 and National Forest Policy 1988; pest control relies on silviculture and integrated pest management.
static.geography: Central Indian sal belt, including Madhya Pradesh.

static.topic: Land Acquisition and Rehabilitation in India
static.syllabusNode: Government Policies and Interventions; Land Reforms
static.whatIsIt: The legal framework under which the state compulsorily acquires private land for a 'public purpose', with mandatory compensation, rehabilitation and resettlement entitlements for affected families.
static.background: Land acquisition in India was long governed by the colonial-era Land Acquisition Act, 1894, criticised for low compensation, weak rehabilitation and frequent litigation. It was replaced by the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, which introduced Social Impact Assessment, consent requirements for public-private partnership and private projects, higher compensation and statutory R&R entitlements. Subsequent central amendment attempts and state-level rules have shaped how the law operates in practice, with states retaining significant latitude in implementation.
static.socioEconomic: Land acquisition is a flashpoint in peri-urban India, where infrastructure, housing and township demand collides with livelihood loss, displacement and prolonged litigation. Compensation norms and consent provisions directly affect the incomes and bargaining power of farmers and small landowners on the urban fringe.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka has issued the final land acquisition notification for the Greater Bengaluru township, advancing the project to the stage where awards and possession follow.
static.wayForward: Publish Social Impact Assessment findings, ensure transparent and time-bound compensation and R&R, exhaust least-displacement alternatives, and align state rules with the 2013 Act's consent and rehabilitation safeguards to reduce litigation.
prelimsPointers: Under the 2013 Act, consent of 70% of affected landowning families is required for PPP projects and 80% for private projects.
Compensation under the 2013 Act is up to four times the market value in rural areas and twice the market value in urban areas.
The 2013 Act mandates a Social Impact Assessment before acquisition in most cases and provides for a multi-tier dispute resolution mechanism.
static.mainsAngle: How far does India's land acquisition law succeed in reconciling the developmental imperative of new townships with the rights and livelihoods of displaced landowners?

static.topic: Metropolitan and Urban Governance in Bengaluru

static.whatIsIt: The institutional arrangement for planning, land use regulation and service delivery across the Bengaluru metropolitan region, involving the state government, municipal corporation(s) and metropolitan planning authorities.
static.background: Bengaluru's civic administration has historically centred on the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike, with metropolitan-level planning handled by the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region Development Authority and land-use regulation flowing from the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act. Expert committee reports have repeatedly recommended unified metropolitan governance with empowered ward-level bodies. Karnataka has since moved to create a Greater Bengaluru Authority as an umbrella body over the city's civic administration, reflecting a wider Indian debate on whether fragmented municipal jurisdictions can manage fast-expanding metros.
static.geography: Bengaluru lies on the Deccan plateau and has expanded outward into surrounding taluks, creating peri-urban belts where planning and service jurisdiction is fragmented between multiple agencies and panchayat bodies.
static.socioEconomic: Outward urban growth reshapes land values, agricultural livelihoods and housing affordability on the city fringe; the quality of metropolitan planning determines whether expansion is serviced and inclusive or speculative and inequitable.
static.whyInNews: The final land acquisition notification for the Greater Bengaluru township is a step in the state's effort to extend planned urban development beyond existing municipal limits.
static.wayForward: Strengthen metropolitan planning capacity, integrate land use with transport and utility networks, fund urban local bodies adequately, and ensure affected peri-urban communities are consulted and rehabilitated.

static.mainsAngle: Fragmented metropolitan governance is a key constraint on Indian urbanisation. Examine with reference to Bengaluru's institutional reforms.

static.topic: Sting Operations, Media Ethics and Investigative Powers
static.syllabusNode: Role of Media; Criminal Justice Administration; Government Policies
static.whatIsIt: Sting operations are covertly recorded investigations used to expose alleged wrongdoing. They raise competing concerns: press freedom and public interest on one side, and privacy, entrapment and fair investigation on the other.
static.background: Covert-camera journalism expanded in India through the 2000s as a tool for exposing corruption, and Indian courts have repeatedly stressed that sting operations must serve genuine public interest and must not violate privacy, induce a person to commit an offence, or amount to entrapment. Alongside this, criminal investigations into such operations are governed by the search, seizure and investigation provisions of the criminal procedure law, which has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

static.whyInNews: The Bengaluru Police's Central Crime Branch searched the residence and office of a Kannada news channel head in connection with an alleged sting operation targeting former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah.
static.wayForward: Media houses should adopt codified ethical standards for covert recording and public-interest justification, while investigating agencies should ensure searches and seizures follow statutory procedure and are seen to be impartial.

static.topic: Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament and State Legislatures: structure, functioning, conduct of business, powers and privileges
static.whatIsIt: The Tenth Schedule to the Constitution, inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985, lays down the grounds on which a member of Parliament or of a State Legislature can be disqualified for defecting from the party on whose ticket he or she was elected.
static.background: Introduced in 1985 during Rajiv Gandhi's government to curb the 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' culture of frequent floor-crossing. The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 removed the earlier exemption for a 'split' by one-third of a legislature party's members, leaving merger (two-thirds) as the only protected route. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the Tenth Schedule but held that the presiding officer's decision is subject to judicial review.
static.whyInNews: Three AAP MLAs from Punjab, including a suspended legislator, joined the BJP ahead of the state assembly elections, reviving debate on defection and party discipline.
static.wayForward: Prescribing a time limit for the presiding officer's decision, considering an independent adjudicatory mechanism, and strengthening inner-party democracy are among the reforms suggested in commission reports and judgments.
prelimsPointers: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985; the 91st Amendment Act, 2003 deleted the one-third 'split' exemption.
A merger is protected only if at least two-thirds of the members of a legislature party agree to it.

static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether the anti-defection law has strengthened party discipline at the cost of legislators' freedom of speech and inner-party democracy.

The announcement was made by the MoES secretary, who framed the expansion as part of strengthening India's earthquake monitoring and hazard-assessment capability. A denser network of seismographs improves the accuracy of locating epicentres, estimating magnitudes and detecting smaller events that sparse coverage can miss. It also feeds into long-term seismic hazard mapping and the scientific basis for building codes and disaster-preparedness planning in high-risk regions. Details on locations, timelines and funding were not specified in the report.
stories.whyItMatters: Earthquake monitoring infrastructure is a core disaster-risk-reduction input: it underpins hazard zonation, early-warning research and building-code enforcement, all of which are recurring UPSC themes under disaster management and geophysical science.

static.topic: National seismic monitoring network in India
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — earthquake monitoring and early warning systems
static.whatIsIt: India operates a national network of seismological observatories that continuously record ground motion, detect earthquakes, determine their epicentre, depth and magnitude, and disseminate information to authorities and the public. The network is coordinated by the National Centre for Seismology (NCS), an attached office under the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES).
static.background: Seismological observation in India dates back to the colonial era, with early observatories established in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; the 1897 Shillong and 1905 Kangra earthquakes spurred scientific interest in Indian seismicity. The network has since been progressively modernised and digitised, with real-time data transmission and automated location of events becoming standard. Despite expansion over the decades, coverage has repeatedly been described in official and scientific discussions as inadequate for a country of India's size and seismic exposure, motivating proposals for further densification.
static.geography: India's seismicity is concentrated along the Himalayan arc (collision boundary of the Indian and Eurasian plates), the Indo-Burman ranges and Northeast India, the Kutch region of Gujarat, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and parts of peninsular India including the Deccan and the Son-Narmada-Tapti lineament zone.
static.socioEconomic: Rapid urbanisation and unregulated construction in seismic zones raise the exposure of population and infrastructure. Better monitoring supports risk-informed land use, insurance pricing, and targeted retrofitting of schools, hospitals and lifeline buildings.
static.whyInNews: The MoES secretary announced a plan to establish 100 new seismic observatories across the country, expanding the existing national network.
static.wayForward: Prioritise siting in under-covered high-risk zones such as the Himalayan belt and Northeast; integrate observatory data with earthquake early-warning research; ensure real-time data sharing with State disaster management authorities; and link monitoring outputs to enforcement of seismic-resistant building codes.
prelimsPointers: The National Centre for Seismology functions under the Ministry of Earth Sciences and maintains the country's seismological network.
Earthquake magnitude is a measure of energy released at the source, while intensity describes the severity of shaking felt at a location.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how densifying the national seismological network can strengthen earthquake risk reduction in India, and examine the institutional and capacity constraints in translating monitoring data into preparedness action.

static.topic: Seismic zoning and earthquake-resistant construction in India
static.syllabusNode: Geography — geophysical phenomena; Disaster Management — mitigation and building codes
static.whatIsIt: India's seismic zoning map, part of the Bureau of Indian Standards code IS 1893, divides the country into four seismic zones — Zone II, III, IV and V — in ascending order of expected shaking hazard. The zoning informs design requirements for structures under the National Building Code and related standards.
static.background: Seismic zoning in India evolved through successive revisions of the BIS earthquake code, with the current four-zone classification replacing an earlier scheme that included a Zone I. Zone V covers the highest-hazard areas, including parts of Northeast India, the Kutch region of Gujarat, parts of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Enforcement of codes rests largely with State and local bodies, and compliance remains uneven.
static.geography: Zone V includes Northeast India, Kutch, parts of the Himalayan states and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands; Zone IV covers parts of the Himalayan foothills, Delhi and adjoining regions; large parts of peninsular India fall in Zones II and III.
static.socioEconomic: Weak code enforcement in fast-growing urban areas is a principal driver of earthquake fatalities; retrofitting and compliance costs compete with short-term construction economics.
static.whyInNews: Expansion of seismic observatory coverage is expected to improve the data base underlying hazard assessment and zoning, which in turn informs building-code requirements.
static.wayForward: Strengthen municipal enforcement capacity, mandate retrofitting of critical infrastructure, and use improved monitoring data to periodically update hazard maps and design codes.
prelimsPointers: India's seismic zoning map has four zones — II, III, IV and V — with Zone V denoting the highest hazard.
The seismic zoning map is published by the Bureau of Indian Standards as part of IS 1893.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why earthquake fatalities in India are driven more by construction practices than by the magnitude of events, and suggest measures to improve compliance with seismic-resistant building standards.
